title: Introducing the 5 Pillars of Data Observability
venue_or_publisher: Monte Carlo blog (page shows 'Updated Aug 02 2022'; original date not shown) [verify original year]
central_claim: Data observability is organised around five pillars: freshness, distribution, volume, schema and lineage, monitored automatically with alerting and triage.
cite_claim: Industrial data observability frames its checks as freshness, distribution, volume, schema and lineage; the article describes monitoring, alerting and triage but no automated fix of producing code.
quote: Volume quite literally refers to the amount of data in a file or database.
relevance: The canonical industry vocabulary. Four of five pillars map to fiks invariants (freshness->D5, volume->D4 countMatchesTotal, schema->D2, distribution->D1). Reviewers will cite this to argue fiks's contract kinds are not new.

title: Monte Carlo Agents (Monitoring, Troubleshooting, Triage, Tuning, PR, Remediation agents)
venue_or_publisher: Monte Carlo product page (undated; sample widget shows dates in Jun-Sep 2026)
central_claim: A fleet of observability agents recommends monitors, finds root causes, triages and tunes alerts, reviews PRs for downstream risk, and a Remediation Agent turns each troubleshooting analysis into a plan that the user's own coding assistant executes via MCP.
cite_claim: The closest industrial loop-closer: Monte Carlo's Remediation Agent produces a root-cause classification and recommended action (code fix or re-run) that a user's coding assistant pulls via MCP; humans stay in the loop and no reproduction-test gate is described. Vendor claims (unaudited): Tuning Agent reduces false positives by 80%+, average data incident takes 19 hours to resolve.
quote: Open the plan in your own AI coding assistant and the agent pulls the full fix via MCP to do the work in your environment.
relevance: Strongest counter-example to 'nobody closes the loop'. fiks must distinguish itself: per-call agent-tool boundary, raw upstream trace, F-gated repro test, gated green-CI PR. MC numbers are marketing, not peer-reviewed; cite as vendor claims only.

title: Data Quality Survey (State of Data Quality 2023)
authors: Monte Carlo; fieldwork by Wakefield Research
central_claim: Survey of 200 data professionals (March 2023): 67 incidents/month, 68% take 4+ hours to detect, average 15 hours to resolve, 74% say business stakeholders find issues first all or most of the time.
cite_claim: In a vendor-commissioned survey (n=200), 74% of data professionals said business stakeholders identify data issues first all or most of the time, and average time to resolution rose to 15 hours per incident.
quote: an astounding 74% reported business stakeholders identify issues first, "all or most of the time,"
relevance: Corroborates C10 (humans catch most silent failures) from the data-pipeline world, but it is vendor-commissioned with an unknown sampling frame; cite as [Secondary-like industry survey].

title: Data Validation for Machine Learning
authors: Eric Breck, Neoklis Polyzotis, Sudip Roy, Steven Euijong Whang, Martin Zinkevich
central_claim: TFX Data Validation infers a schema from data, validates every batch, detects training/serving and distribution skew with an L-infinity distance (not significance tests), and routes alerts to on-call humans who either fix data generation or update the schema.
cite_claim: A chi-square skew test on 100M points with 0.01% injected noise would 'needlessly fire an alert 7 out of 10 times', so TFDV uses the L-infinity distance with a human-set threshold; on-calls ignore spammy or non-actionable alerts; after an alert the user either fixes the data generation process or updates the schema.
location: Sec. 1 (Example 1.1 discussion); Sec. 4 'Quantifying Distribution Distance' and Fig. 5; Sec. 3 schema inference; Sec. 6.1 and Table 1
quote: this method would needlessly fire an alert 7 out of 10 times and would most likely be considered a flaky detection method.
relevance: Deep-read. Strongest primary evidence that statistical drift tests are FP-prone at scale and that overfitted auto-schemas cause spurious alerts that make users switch validation off. Shows the industrial loop ends at a human fixing code ('isolate the bug in the code, and submit a fix'). Same key as spec-inference.md; URL now points to the full-text PDF.

title: Data Lifecycle Challenges in Production Machine Learning: A Survey
authors: Neoklis Polyzotis, Sudip Roy, Steven Euijong Whang, Martin Zinkevich
central_claim: Data validation must balance alert precision and recall; an alert is a 'good catch' only if it is actionable and eventually leads to a fix; distribution-shift alerts are often less actionable than missing-feature alerts.
cite_claim: Over-alerting leads users to ignore all alerts; the authors define alert precision as the fraction of alerts that are actionable and lead to a fix, and argue the question is whether an alert gets fixed, not only whether something is wrong.
quote: Hence, the question is not whether something is wrong if an alert fires, but whether it gets fixed.
relevance: Deep-read. Gives fiks a principled metric from the data-validation literature: alert-to-fix conversion. fiks makes the fix part of the system. Also flags the constraint-vs-data ambiguity (new value 'SS' could be South Sudan): a violation may mean the contract should change, not the code.

title: The ML Test Score: A Rubric for ML Production Readiness and Technical Debt Reduction
authors: Eric Breck, Shanqing Cai, Eric Nielsen, Michael Salib, D. Sculley
venue_or_publisher: IEEE International Conference on Big Data 2017
central_claim: 28 tests and monitors for production ML, including Data 1 (feature expectations captured in a schema), Monitor 1 (dependency changes result in notification) and Monitor 2 (data invariants hold in training and serving inputs).
cite_claim: Monitor 1 warns that version upgrades in a source system can radically change a feature's meaning without producing values strange enough to trigger other monitoring; its remedy is a human process (subscribe to announcement lists). Monitor 2 says alert thresholds need careful tuning to balance false positives and negatives.
location: Sec. on Monitoring tests, Monitor 1 and Monitor 2; Data 1 and Table I
quote: version upgrades, and other changes in the source system can radically change the feature's meaning ... without necessarily producing values that are strange enough
relevance: Deep-read (PDF). Names exactly fiks's D1/D5 class (semantic drift from upstream version upgrades with plausible values) a decade-old known problem in ML systems, and documents that the recommended fix is organisational, not automated.

title: Automating Large-Scale Data Quality Verification (Deequ)
authors: Sebastian Schelter, Dustin Lange, Philipp Schmidt, Meltem Celikel, Felix Biessmann, Andreas Grafberger
central_claim: Declarative unit tests for data plus heuristic constraint suggestion from column profiles and anomaly detection on metric time series.
cite_claim: Deequ suggests constraints (completeness, type, range, uniqueness, categorical domain) from profiles and relies on users to vet them; see spec-inference.md for the 10/90 held-out suggestion results.
location: Sec. 3.3, Sec. 5.3, Table 3 (as recorded in spec-inference.sources.json; not re-read here)
quote: rely on the end user to select from and validate our suggestions which might not necessarily hold for future data
relevance: Reused key from spec-inference.md (not re-read in this pass). The profiler-generated baseline for H15 and HD1.

title: Test data quality at scale with Deequ
authors: Philipp Schmidt, Ginni Malik, Dustin Lange, Neha Bhupatiraju, Sebastian Schelter, Tammo Rukat
venue_or_publisher: AWS Big Data Blog (2019-05-16; March 2023 update notes AWS Glue Data Quality is built on Deequ)
central_claim: Deequ, used at Amazon, computes data-quality metrics, verifies constraints, suggests constraints by profiling, and runs anomaly detection on metrics over time; AWS Glue Data Quality is built on it.
cite_claim: Deequ's constraint suggestions are based on heuristic rules and assume the data shown is correct, so they must be reviewed before production use.
quote: based on heuristic rules and assumes that the data it is shown is correct
relevance: Industrial deployment evidence for profiler-generated constraints; the 'assumes the data is correct' caveat is the same clean-history assumption fiks's inferred-contract experiment (H15) must make explicit.

title: Auto-Validate by-History: Auto-Program Data Quality Constraints to Validate Recurring Data Pipelines
authors: Dezhan Tu, Yeye He, Weiwei Cui, Song Ge, Haidong Zhang, Han Shi, Dongmei Zhang, Surajit Chaudhuri
central_claim: Infers conjunctive single-column DQ programs (row count, complete ratio, unique ratio, min/max/mean, EMD/JS/KL/KS distances) from the history of recurring pipelines, choosing constraints to maximise recall under a user-set expected-FPR budget with Chebyshev/Cantelli/CLT bounds; evaluated on 2,000 Microsoft production pipelines.
cite_claim: Data-quality issues creep into recurring pipelines through upstream schema and data drift; AVH programs constraints from history with an FPR target and reports outperforming Deequ, TFDV (high precision, low recall) and anomaly-detection baselines; it assumes the history is clean and only alerts.
location: Abstract; Sec. 3 (Tables 1-2 metrics); Sec. 4.1-4.3 (FPR bounds); Sec. 5.1 setup; Sec. 5.3 and Figs. 2-3; App. J, L
quote: data quality (DQ) issues can often creep into recurring pipelines because of upstream schema and data drift over time
relevance: Deep-read. The state of the art for 'infer contracts from v1 history with a controlled FPR'. Directly the inference baseline/rival for H15; its FPR-budget formulation is a method fiks could adopt. Single-column only; cannot express read-after-write or cross-field countMatchesTotal.

title: Auto-Validate: Unsupervised Data Validation Using Data-Domain Patterns Inferred from Data Lakes
central_claim: Corpus-driven inference of string data-domain patterns that minimise false positives while catching quality issues; part shipped as Auto-Tag in Azure Purview.
cite_claim: Pattern-based validation for machine-generated string columns can be inferred from a data-lake corpus, aiming to minimise false positives; parts ship in Azure Purview.
quote: while maximizing data quality issues caught
relevance: Format drift (e.g., D5 timestamp ISO->epoch-ms string shape) is the kind of change pattern inference catches; a candidate inference baseline for string-shaped fields. Abstract-level only.

title: Moving Fast With Broken Data (CIKM 2023 version: 'Automatic and Precise Data Validation for Machine Learning' [verify title mapping])
authors: Shreya Shankar, Labib Fawaz, Karl Gyllstrom, Aditya G. Parameswaran
central_claim: At Meta, schema validation is necessary but not sufficient; completeness thresholds, z-score and KS-test partition validation produced many false positives that engineers silenced; GATE improves precision 2.1x on average over the baseline in an Instagram case study.
cite_claim: A 30% completeness-drop threshold produced too many false-positive alerts; ML engineers silenced the alerts and eventually abandoned that validation method; z-score and KS tests also yielded many false positives at high recall.
quote: none of the methods by themselves met our requirements for high precision and recall in detecting corruptions
relevance: Deep-read. Best published industrial evidence of alert fatigue killing data validation. Supports reporting per-receipt FP on clean traffic as a first-class metric (H5) and choosing deterministic semantic contracts over statistical tests for per-call checks.

title: Operationalizing Machine Learning: An Interview Study
authors: Shreya Shankar, Rolando Garcia, Joseph M. Hellerstein, Aditya G. Parameswaran
central_claim: Interviews with 18 ML engineers find production ML success governed by Velocity, Validation and Versioning, with monitoring of production performance drops part of a continual loop.
cite_claim: Practitioners treat validation and production monitoring as a continual loop in MLOps (18 interviews).
quote: monitoring of performance drops in production
relevance: Context only; abstract-level read. Alert-fatigue details in the body were not re-checked here [verify before citing for alert fatigue].

title: Data drift: how Evidently detects drift (explainer)
central_claim: Default per-column drift test depends on type and reference size: KS (numerical) or chi-squared (categorical) at p<=0.05 when reference <=1000 rows; Wasserstein (numerical) or Jensen-Shannon (categorical) with threshold 0.1 above 1000 rows; dataset drift is a share-of-drifted-columns rule.
cite_claim: Evidently's default drift detection uses KS/chi-squared for references of at most 1000 rows and Wasserstein/Jensen-Shannon with a 0.1 threshold above that; by default drift tests do not react to rising null counts.
location: Sections 'Tabular data drift' defaults; dataset drift; note on nulls
quote: By default, drift tests do not react to changes or increases in the number of empty values.
relevance: Defines the runnable D1/D5 distribution-shift baseline exactly. Important: defaults ignore null-rate increases, so D2 (null price) needs a separate null-share test; distribution tests need a window of calls, not a single call.

title: Which test is the best? We compared 5 methods to detect data drift on large datasets
central_claim: On large samples KS flags minor changes (0.5% shift above 100,000 objects); PSI is insensitive; Wasserstein with a 0.1 threshold is a reasonable default.
cite_claim: KS raises drift flags for a 0.5% change once a dataset exceeds 100,000 objects, so drift-test choice and sample size dominate false-positive behaviour.
quote: It raises flags even for a minor change of 0.5%, as soon as we have more than 100,000 objects in a dataset.
relevance: Vendor experiment (not peer-reviewed) replicating the TFDV observation; supports a pre-registered choice of Wasserstein/JS defaults for the Evidently baseline and a v1b benign-drift FP test.

title: evidentlyai/evidently
central_claim: Open-source (Apache-2.0) framework to evaluate, test and monitor ML and LLM systems with 100+ metrics; reports become pass/fail test suites with conditions; 20+ drift tests.
cite_claim: Evidently is Apache-2.0, pip-installable, and turns drift and data-quality reports (missing values, ranges, new categories) into pass/fail test suites.
quote: An open-source framework to evaluate, test and monitor ML and LLM-powered systems.
relevance: Runnable baseline for HD1/HD2 (distribution-shift detector on flattened tool results).

title: Great Expectations core expectations (great_expectations/expectations/core/__init__.py) and GX Core repository
central_claim: GX Core (Apache-2.0) provides 'unit tests for your data' as Expectations; the core set includes ExpectColumnValuesToBeBetween, ExpectColumnValuesToNotBeNull, ExpectTableRowCountToEqualOtherTable, ExpectTableColumnsToMatchSet, ExpectColumnKLDivergenceToBeLessThan, ExpectColumnValuesToMatchStrftimeFormat, ExpectColumnValuesToMatchJsonSchema, ExpectColumnValuesToBeUnique, and 60 classes in all.
cite_claim: Every fiks single-result invariant kind except read-after-write and equalsUpstream has a direct GX core analogue (range, notNull, row count vs another table, unique, JSON schema, date format; freshness via max-date bounds).
quote: expressive and extensible unit tests for your data
relevance: Concedes the vocabulary overlap concretely; GX is the runnable rule-based baseline (Apache-2.0).

title: GX V0 to V1 Migration Guide
central_claim: Profilers (incl. data assistants) were removed in GX V1, to be re-introduced later.
cite_claim: GX V1 removed profilers, so an auto-profiled GX baseline must either pin GX 0.18 or generate expectations with our own Deequ-style profiler.
quote: This feature has been removed in V1. Some form of profilers will be re-introduced in V1 at a later date.
relevance: Practical constraint on building the 'GX auto-profiled on v1' baseline; prefer a transparent in-house profiler emitting GX expectations, or pin GX 0.18.x [verify last 0.x version].

title: SodaCL freshness checks
central_claim: A freshness check measures the age of the most recent row in a timestamp/date column against scan time, e.g. freshness(start_date) < 3d.
cite_claim: Soda expresses freshness as the age of the newest timestamp relative to scan time, the same semantics as fiks's freshness invariant (maxAgeDays).
location: Freshness checks page, syntax and details
quote: freshness(start_date) < 3d
relevance: D5 (epoch-ms parsed as 1970) would fail a Soda freshness check exactly as it fails fiks's; another instance of vocabulary overlap.

title: SodaCL anomaly detection checks
central_claim: Prophet-based anomaly detection on metric time series; needs at least four regular measurements; default interval_width 0.999; pattern changes can trigger consecutive false positives and parameters may need tuning to prevent alert fatigue; user feedback can exclude anomalies.
cite_claim: Soda's own docs warn that pattern changes can cause consecutive false positives and that parameters may need adjusting to prevent alert fatigue; detection needs at least four measurements first.
location: Anomaly detection page: requirements, sensitivity tuning, feedback
quote: you may need to adjust the default parameters to improve the model's ability to detect anomalies to prevent alert fatigue.
relevance: Time-series anomaly detection needs history (>=4 regular scans) before it can fire; fiks fires on the first violating call. Supports the calls-to-detection hypothesis (HD2).

title: sodadata/soda-core
central_claim: Soda Core is a data quality and data contract verification engine with YAML contracts (schema, row_count, missing, invalid) and 50+ built-in checks; main branch licensed under Elastic License 2.0.
cite_claim: Soda Core's current main branch is under the Elastic License 2.0, not an OSI licence; anomaly detection is a Soda Cloud feature.
quote: a data quality and data contract verification engine
relevance: Licence matters for a baseline: usable for evaluation but not OSI; prefer GX/Evidently/whylogs as primary baselines [verify v3 licence was Apache-2.0].

title: Add data tests to your DAG
central_claim: dbt ships four generic data tests (unique, not_null, accepted_values, relationships); each test is a SELECT returning failing rows, with severity and warn_if/error_if thresholds.
cite_claim: dbt data tests are SQL queries that return failing rows; zero rows means the assertion holds.
quote: If the data test returns zero failing rows, it passes, and your assertion has been validated.
relevance: Shows declarative invariants are standard in analytics engineering; dbt tests run on batches in a warehouse, not on per-call tool results.

title: Source freshness (dbt platform)
central_claim: dbt computes source freshness against an SLA; dbt build does not include freshness checks; freshness jobs should run at least twice as often as the lowest SLA.
cite_claim: dbt source freshness is a scheduled job compared to an SLA and is not part of dbt build.
quote: you should run your source freshness jobs with at least double the frequency of your lowest SLA
relevance: Freshness is a load-time property of a table in dbt; in fiks it is a property of a field in one tool result. loaded_at_field/warn_after config keys come from the sources docs, not re-read here [verify].

title: Model contracts
central_claim: dbt model contracts enforce column names, data types and platform-supported constraints at build time and fail the build on mismatch; content quality is left to data tests.
cite_claim: dbt separates structural contracts (names, types, constraints, enforced at build) from content checks (data tests), the same split as MCP outputSchema versus fiks's semantic invariants.
location: Page body: enforcement, data tests vs contracts
quote: or it will fail to build
relevance: Precedent for fiks's layering argument (C4/C26): structural contract floor plus semantic checks.

title: Open Data Contract Standard (ODCS)
authors: Bitol project, LF AI & Data Foundation
central_claim: ODCS v3.2.0 (Apache-2.0) is a YAML standard for producer-consumer data contracts covering schema, data quality, SLA, support, pricing, roles and servers.
cite_claim: Data contracts are standardised (ODCS v3.2.0 under LF AI & Data) as an agreement between a data producer and consumers, with schema, quality and SLA sections.
quote: the agreement between a data producer and consumers
relevance: fiks contracts are consumer-side outcome contracts for tool results; ODCS is the closest standard. Possible export target so fiks contracts interoperate with datacontract-cli.

title: ODCS Data Quality section
central_claim: Quality rules are text, library metrics (nullValues, missingValues, invalidValues, duplicateValues, rowCount), SQL or custom engine (e.g. soda, greatExpectations), with operators mustBe, mustBeBetween, etc.
cite_claim: ODCS library quality metrics include nullValues, invalidValues, duplicateValues and rowCount with mustBe/mustBeBetween thresholds, delegating custom checks to engines such as Soda or Great Expectations.
location: Data quality page: rule types; operators
quote: Any value is authorized here.
relevance: fiks range/notNull/unique/nonEmpty map to ODCS invalidValues/nullValues/duplicateValues/rowCount; read-after-write and equalsUpstream have no ODCS library metric.

title: datacontract/datacontract-cli
central_claim: MIT-licensed CLI that tests data against ODCS contracts (schema and quality) on ~20 sources and detects breaking changes between contract versions (datacontract breaking).
cite_claim: datacontract-cli tests live data against an ODCS contract and flags breaking changes between two contract versions; like oasdiff, the breaking check compares contracts, not observed behaviour.
quote: [no verbatim quote recorded; README documents the test and breaking commands] [verify]
relevance: Runnable (MIT) data-contract baseline; its 'breaking' command is a spec-diff and would not fire on fiks's seeded drifts where the vendor spec is unchanged (consistent with C27/H2).

title: Autothresholds
central_claim: Learned thresholds from 21 days of history (three cycles for seasonality), retuned every 24 hours, with sensitivity levels; closing an issue as 'bad alert' adds the points to training and widens sensitivity.
cite_claim: Bigeye autothresholds learn from a default 21-day window and use user feedback on bad alerts to widen thresholds, i.e. FP control by human feedback.
location: Autothresholds page: training window; sensitivity; feedback
quote: three or more cycles
relevance: Shows learned-threshold monitors need weeks of history and human feedback; a benign v1b change (e.g., real price rise) is either an FP or, after 'adapt', absorbed, which is the same mechanism that would absorb a silent unit drift if a user marked it as normal.

title: Anomalo product site and 'Automating Data Quality Monitoring: Scaling Beyond Rules With Machine Learning' (O'Reilly book, blog series)
central_claim: Unsupervised ML builds baselines of table characteristics to catch issues no one wrote rules for; agents monitor freshness, schema and natural-language quality definitions; a planned first-responder agent opens tickets (ServiceNow, JIRA) rather than fixing code.
cite_claim: Anomalo argues unsupervised ML catches errors teams would never have written rules for; its remediation path is tickets and escalation to people, not code fixes.
location: Book chapter 1 post; homepage agent descriptions (https://www.anomalo.com/)
quote: would never have thought to set up rules to check
relevance: Strongest version of the 'ML monitors beat hand rules' argument (the vocabulary-limit critique, C11). No published FP rate found.

title: whylabs/whylogs
central_claim: Apache-2.0 library that logs compact statistical profiles of data for drift tracking, constraints and visualisation.
cite_claim: whylogs profiles data into mergeable statistical summaries and supports constraints and drift detection; Apache-2.0.
quote: [no verbatim quote recorded; README describes profiles for tracking changes, constraints and visualisation] [verify]
relevance: Lightweight runnable alternative to Evidently for per-window profiles of tool results; company status (WhyLabs platform) not verified here.

title: Elementary volume_anomalies test
central_claim: dbt-native volume anomaly test: daily buckets, 14-day training period, 2-day detection period, only completed buckets evaluated.
cite_claim: Elementary's dbt volume anomaly test trains on 14 days of bucketed row counts and evaluates only completed buckets.
quote: The test will only run on completed time buckets.
relevance: Concrete detection-latency floor for volume monitors (days); fiks's countMatchesTotal fires on the first truncated response (D4).

title: How is ChatGPT's behavior changing over time?
authors: Lingjiao Chen, Matei Zaharia, James Zou
venue_or_publisher: arXiv:2307.09009 (v3, 2023-10-31); also Harvard Data Science Review 2024 [verify]
central_claim: The same named LLM API (GPT-4, GPT-3.5) changed behaviour substantially between March and June 2023: GPT-4 prime identification 84.0% -> 51.1%; directly executable code 52.0% -> 10.0%.
cite_claim: Behaviour of a named LLM service can change greatly within months without a version change visible to users (GPT-4 directly-executable code generations 52.0% -> 10.0%), and the authors call for continuous monitoring.
location: Abstract; Sec. 3.1 (Math I); Sec. 3.5 / Fig. 9 (code); Sec. 5
quote: the behavior of the "same" LLM service can change substantially in a relatively short amount of time
relevance: Deep-read. LLM-API behaviour drift is upstream drift under an unchanged interface, the same structure as fiks's vendor drift. But fiks's deterministic contracts fit structured outputs, not stochastic text quality; this is a scope boundary. Quote verified against the arXiv abstract on 2026-10-21.

title: Model Equality Testing: Which Model Is This API Serving?
authors: Irena Gao, Percy Liang, Carlos Guestrin
central_claim: Detecting a changed API model is a two-sample test; an MMD string-kernel test reaches median 77.4% power with ~10 samples per prompt; 11 of 31 Llama endpoints served a different distribution than reference weights.
cite_claim: Distributional audits of LLM APIs need repeated samples per prompt and found 11 of 31 commercial Llama endpoints deviating from the reference distribution.
quote: We formalize detecting such distortions as Model Equality Testing, a two-sample testing problem.
relevance: Statistical drift detection for stochastic upstreams needs many samples; fiks's per-call deterministic checks do not, but only cover declared invariants.

title: Are You Getting What You Pay For? Auditing Model Substitution in LLM APIs
authors: Will Cai, Tianneng Shi, Xuandong Zhao, Dawn Song
central_claim: Output-based statistical tests need many queries and miss subtle model substitutions; log-prob methods fail under inference nondeterminism; the authors propose TEEs.
cite_claim: Software-only output monitoring cannot reliably detect subtle upstream model substitution; log-probability methods are defeated by production nondeterminism.
quote: methods using log probabilities are defeated by inherent inference nondeterminism in production environments
relevance: Limits of black-box drift detection; supports stating that fiks targets deterministic structured fields where single-call checks are decisive, and is not an LLM-drift detector.

title: Failing Loudly: An Empirical Study of Methods for Detecting Dataset Shift
authors: Stephan Rabanser, Stephan Gunnemann, Zachary C. Lipton
central_claim: Across studied shifts, two-sample testing on representations from pre-trained classifiers performs best; domain discriminators help characterise shifts.
cite_claim: The standard empirical study of shift detectors finds two-sample tests on classifier-reduced representations work best.
quote: a two-sample-testing-based approach, using pre-trained classifiers for dimensionality reduction, performs best
relevance: Foundational reference for the distribution-shift baseline family; per-method results not re-read [verify before citing details].
